## 8. Models

<!-- models:start (generated by tools/process_models.mjs; edit outside these markers) -->

### Lego Voxel (`lumenary:lego-voxel`, models this process)

_From: Toy bricks and voxel graphics; when: 1958 brick, 2010s voxel art; works best on: Bold, colourful subjects and simple faces._

A brick mosaic is a palette problem. Each stud can only be one of the colours that bricks come in, so the picture is rebuilt from a small, fixed set. A little ordered dithering lets a smooth gradient become a mix of two neighbouring brick colours, and the drawn studs with their shadows and shine make it feel like plastic.

**How it is made, as the model does it:**

1. Reduce the picture to one pixel per stud, each the average of its patch.
2. Add a small offset from a 4 × 4 Bayer pattern so gradients mix two brick colours.
3. Replace each stud with the nearest brick colour, using a weighting that favours red in bright colours and blue in dark ones.
4. Draw each stud as a short cylinder with a shadow, a darker side, a lighter top and a pale arc of shine.
5. Give each brick a light top and left edge and a dark bottom and right edge.

**The maths:**

$$d^2=\Big(2+\frac{\bar r}{256}\Big)\Delta R^2+4\,\Delta G^2+\Big(2+\frac{255-\bar r}{256}\Big)\Delta B^2,\qquad \bar r=\frac{R_1+R_2}{2}$$

_The “redmean” colour distance._ (primitives: palette-snap)

$$C_{\text{stud}}\in\{0.74\,C,\ 1.07\,C\}$$

_The side of the stud is drawn at 74% of the brick colour and the top at 107%._ (primitives: facet-shading)

**Dials:** `studs` (Studs across) = 40 [16 to 96]; `palette` (Brick colours) = "full" (full, basic, greys); `dither` (Dither tones) = 30 [0 to 100]; `shine` (Shine) = true.

**History:** The LEGO brick in its modern interlocking form was patented in 1958 in Denmark. Mosaics from plates of single-colour studs became a hobby of their own, and LEGO later sold sets that build art from them. A voxel is a pixel with volume, and games such as Minecraft turned the idea of a world made of cubes into mainstream culture.
